title: Solar particle event — take shelter
what: A solar particle event (SPE) is in progress: a burst of high-energy protons from the Sun. Dose rates in lightly shielded areas can rise sharply within hours.
whySpace: Outside Earth's magnetic field nothing stops SPE protons except the vehicle's own shielding. NASA requires protecting crew from a design-reference SPE to below 250 mSv. Early alerts let the crew reach shielding before most of the dose arrives; a storm shelter of about 10 cm water-equivalent, built from water containers and stowage, is the recommended approach.
doNow: Move to the designated storm shelter area now
Stay until the event-end notice
Log time spent outside shelter
source: NASA-STD-3001 Vol 1 Rev C [V1 4031]; NASA-STD-3001 Technical Brief OCHMO-TB-020 Radiation Protection

title: Projected mission dose above career limit
what: At the published dose rate for this environment, total mission dose is projected to pass NASA's 600 mSv career limit before the mission ends.
whySpace: Galactic cosmic rays cannot be fully shielded and add dose every day of the mission. NASA caps career effective dose below 600 mSv for every astronaut to limit long-term cancer risk, and requires exposure to be kept as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA).
doNow: Spend sleep and off-duty time in the best-shielded areas (crew quarters, near water and stowage)
Compare personal dosimeter readings with this projection
Flag the projection in the next report to ground for mission-plan review
source: NASA-STD-3001 Vol 1 Rev C [V1 4029] ALARA, [V1 4030] career limit < 600 mSv

title: Heart rate or blood pressure above your baseline
what: Resting heart rate or systolic blood pressure is above your personal pre-flight baseline.
whySpace: Weightlessness shifts body fluids toward the head and changes how the heart and blood vessels work. NASA tracks this as a spaceflight risk: it can contribute to heart rhythm problems in flight and to low blood pressure and fainting on return to gravity.
doNow: Rest quietly for 10 minutes, then re-measure
Drink water and skip caffeine until the re-check
Note any dizziness, chest discomfort or palpitations and tell the crew medical officer
source: NASA Human Research Program — Risk of Cardiovascular Adaptations

title: Low heart rate variability
what: Heart rate variability (HRV) is trending below your personal baseline. Low HRV is a general sign of stress, fatigue or incomplete recovery — not a diagnosis on its own.
whySpace: Heavy workload, shifting schedules and broken sleep are common in flight, and NASA lists sleep loss, circadian disruption and work overload as risks to crew performance. HRV is a cheap daily signal that recovery is falling behind.
doNow: Do a 5-minute slow-breathing session (about 6 breaths per minute)
Protect tonight's sleep window
Re-measure tomorrow morning before exercise or caffeine
source: NASA Human Research Program — Risk from Inadequate Sleep and Irregular Schedules (HRV as a recovery marker is general physiology practice, not a NASA requirement)

title: Sleep deficit / low mood
what: Sleep duration or your mood check-in has been below your personal baseline for several days.
whySpace: Astronauts average about 6 hours of sleep in flight, against the 7–9 hours adults need. After a week of 6-hour nights, performance can drop to the level of 24–36 hours without sleep, and sleep loss also lowers mood. On the ISS the crew sees 16 sunrises a day, which confuses the body clock.
doNow: Protect a full 8-hour sleep window tonight: lights off, eye mask, earplugs
Dim screens and cabin light for the hour before sleep; no caffeine late in the day
Talk with a crewmate, or book a private conference with the ground support team
source: NASA-STD-3001 Technical Brief: Sleep Accommodations (Rev A); OCHMO-TB-014 Behavioral Health Mishaps

title: Exercise below target
what: Daily exercise time is below your personal baseline.
whySpace: Without gravity loading, bone, muscle and aerobic fitness decline quickly. NASA requires in-flight countermeasures to keep muscle strength and aerobic capacity at or above 80% of pre-flight values, and hip and spine bone density at or above 95%. Exercise is the main countermeasure.
doNow: Make up the missed resistance session today
Add a cardio block (treadmill or cycle) to the next exercise slot
Log why the session was missed so ground can adjust the schedule
source: NASA-STD-3001 Vol 1 Rev C [V1 4003], [V1 4024], [V1 4027]; Technical Brief OCHMO-TB-031 Exercise Overview

title: Change in near vision
what: Your near-vision self-check score is below your personal baseline.
whySpace: Weightlessness shifts fluid toward the head, which can cause optic nerve swelling, retinal folds and flattening of the back of the eye — spaceflight associated neuro-ocular syndrome (SANS). About 70% of ISS astronauts show some swelling at the back of the eye, and the risk grows with mission length.
doNow: Repeat the near-vision check in good light, one eye at a time
Note headaches or blurred or distorted vision, and when they started
Request an onboard eye exam (acuity, Amsler grid, imaging if available) and send results to ground
source: NASA Human Research Program — Risk of Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS)
